prompt: What does branching make possible that working in a single line of history does not?
optionA: Keeping a spare copy of the project in case of accident
optionB: Carrying unfinished work forward without disturbing the version that already works
optionC: Giving each person on the team a project of their own
optionD: Storing files that are too large to record
correctAnswerText: Carrying unfinished work forward without disturbing the version that already works
explanation: A branch lets half-done work be recorded and returned to, so it allows carrying unfinished work forward without disturbing the version that already works. In one line, unfinished work and working code have to share the same commits.

prompt: Is a branch a copy of the project folder?
optionA: Yes; each branch gets a folder of its own
optionB: Yes, though only the changed files are duplicated
optionC: No; it is a copy of the most recent commit
optionD: No; it is a second line of history over the same folder
correctAnswerText: No; it is a second line of history over the same folder
explanation: There is one folder and one recorded history, so a branch is a second line of history over the same folder. Believing it duplicates the project is what makes branching feel expensive.

prompt: Two features are being built at the same time. What does giving each one a branch achieve?
optionA: Either can be finished and recorded without the other's half-done work coming with it
optionB: Each feature gets a separate backup
optionC: Each feature gets its own shared copy
optionD: The two features are combined automatically when they are done
correctAnswerText: Either can be finished and recorded without the other's half-done work coming with it
explanation: The two sets of commits stay apart until somebody joins them, so either can be finished and recorded without the other's half-done work coming with it. Nothing is combined until a merge is asked for.

prompt: Can work done on a branch be brought back into the main line later?
optionA: No; a branch is a permanent separation
optionB: Only by copying the files across by hand
optionC: Yes; merging is what joins the two histories
optionD: Only if no further commits were made on the main line
correctAnswerText: Yes; merging is what joins the two histories
explanation: Branches are made to be rejoined, and merging is what joins the two histories. Commits made on the main line in the meantime do not prevent it.

prompt: Why is a branch preferred to simply keeping a second copy of the folder while an experiment is tried?
optionA: A branch takes up less room on the disk
optionB: The two histories can be recombined afterwards, which two folders cannot be
optionC: A branch is quicker to switch between
optionD: A branch cannot produce a clash
correctAnswerText: The two histories can be recombined afterwards, which two folders cannot be
explanation: Two folders leave somebody comparing files by hand at the end, whereas the two histories can be recombined afterwards, which two folders cannot be. Space and speed are side effects rather than the reason.

prompt: What is created at the moment a new branch is made?
optionA: A copy of every file in the project
optionB: A new folder alongside the existing one
optionC: A new shared copy of the project
optionD: A name that points at the commit you are currently on
correctAnswerText: A name that points at the commit you are currently on
explanation: Making a branch records a name that points at the commit you are currently on and nothing else. That is why it is instant however large the project is.

prompt: Do the files in the working folder change at the moment a branch is created?
optionA: No; nothing changes until commits are made or another branch is switched to
optionB: Yes; they are reset to the last recorded state
optionC: Yes; a second set of them appears
optionD: Yes; any unrecorded work is cleared away first
correctAnswerText: No; nothing changes until commits are made or another branch is switched to
explanation: Creating a branch is a note about history rather than an operation on files, so nothing changes until commits are made or another branch is switched to. Unrecorded work is left exactly where it was.

prompt: Does creating a branch require a shared copy of the project?
optionA: Yes; branches exist on the shared copy
optionB: Yes, unless the project has never been shared at all
optionC: No; branches are local until somebody sends them
optionD: Only the first branch requires one
correctAnswerText: No; branches are local until somebody sends them
explanation: Branching is a local act like committing, so branches are local until somebody sends them. A project that has never been shared can have as many as it likes.

prompt: A project of 500 files has six branches. How many copies of those files are sitting on the disk?
optionA: Six, one for each branch
optionB: One working folder, plus one recorded history that all six branches read from
optionC: Six, but only of the files that differ between branches
optionD: Three thousand, one set per branch
correctAnswerText: One working folder, plus one recorded history that all six branches read from
explanation: Branches are names into a single recorded history, so there is one working folder, plus one recorded history that all six branches read from. The count of branches has almost no bearing on the size of the project.

prompt: What does a merge produce?
optionA: A third branch holding the work of both
optionB: Two branches that are now identical
optionC: One branch holding whichever work was newer
optionD: One branch that now holds the work of both
correctAnswerText: One branch that now holds the work of both
explanation: Merging joins one line into another, leaving one branch that now holds the work of both. No third branch is created and nothing is chosen on grounds of age.

prompt: A branch called feature is merged into a branch called main. Which of the two changes?
optionA: main only
optionB: Both of them
optionC: feature only
optionD: Neither; a new branch receives the result
correctAnswerText: main only
explanation: A merge has a direction, and the work travels into the branch being merged into, so main only changes. feature is left exactly as it was.

prompt: Does merging a branch remove that branch?
optionA: Yes, as part of the merge
optionB: Yes, once it has no commits left to contribute
optionC: No; it stays exactly where it was
optionD: Yes, as soon as the merge is sent to the shared copy
correctAnswerText: No; it stays exactly where it was
explanation: A merge copies work into another line and leaves the source alone, so the branch stays exactly where it was. Deleting it afterwards is a separate decision somebody makes.

prompt: After feature has been merged into main, which branches hold the feature work?
optionA: main only, because the work moved there
optionB: Both, since main received a copy and feature still has its own
optionC: feature only, until main is sent
optionD: A new branch created by the merge
correctAnswerText: Both, since main received a copy and feature still has its own
explanation: Merging copies rather than moves, so both hold the work: main received a copy and feature still has its own. What feature does not have is anything main gained from elsewhere.

prompt: You switch to a branch called feature and make two commits. Which branch holds them?
optionA: main, because that is the project's real line
optionB: Both, since they are commits to the same project
optionC: Neither, until they are merged somewhere
optionD: feature
correctAnswerText: feature
explanation: Commits land on whichever branch is current at the time, so feature holds them. They reach anywhere else only through a merge.

prompt: The sequence was: on main, commit A; switch to feature, commit B; switch back to main, commit C. Which commits does main hold?
optionA: A and C
optionB: A, B and C
optionC: A only
optionD: B and C
correctAnswerText: A and C
explanation: B was made while feature was current and the other two while main was, so main holds A and C. Switching away and back does not carry work with it.

prompt: A file was added and committed on feature. You switch to main, where that file was never created. What is in the folder?
optionA: The file is still there, since it exists on the disk
optionB: The file is there but empty
optionC: The file is not there, because the folder now shows what main holds
optionD: The switch is refused while that file exists
correctAnswerText: The file is not there, because the folder now shows what main holds
explanation: Switching rewrites the working folder to match the branch being switched to, so the file is not there, because the folder now shows what main holds. The folder always reflects one branch at a time.

prompt: That file has vanished from the folder after the switch. Has the work been lost?
optionA: Yes; switching discarded it
optionB: No; it is recorded on the other branch and reappears on switching back
optionC: Yes, unless it had been sent to the shared copy first
optionD: No; it is still in the folder but hidden from view
correctAnswerText: No; it is recorded on the other branch and reappears on switching back
explanation: Being absent from the folder and being lost are different things: it is recorded on the other branch and reappears on switching back. Only unrecorded work is ever at risk here.

prompt: Three commits are made on feature. What does main hold afterwards?
optionA: The three commits as well
optionB: The newest of the three commits
optionC: Nothing, until it is brought up to date
optionD: Exactly what it held before
correctAnswerText: Exactly what it held before
explanation: Work on one branch has no effect on another, so main holds exactly what it held before. It is older than feature rather than out of date in any broken sense.

prompt: Both branches contain a file called config.txt. The copy on feature is edited and committed. What does the copy on main contain?
optionA: Its own version, unchanged
optionB: The edited version, since the two files share a name
optionC: An empty file, until the branches are merged
optionD: The edited version, marked as coming from another branch
correctAnswerText: Its own version, unchanged
explanation: A shared name does not make a shared file across two lines of history, so the copy on main holds its own version, unchanged. The two versions meet only in a merge.

prompt: A teammate says main is out of date, because feature has newer commits on it. Is anything wrong with main?
optionA: Yes; the newest commits anywhere are the real state of the project
optionB: Yes; main has to be brought up to date before it can be used
optionC: No; main is a different line, and being newer does not make feature authoritative
optionD: No; main will catch up by itself once feature is sent
correctAnswerText: No; main is a different line, and being newer does not make feature authoritative
explanation: Newer and correct are different claims, so nothing is wrong: main is a different line, and being newer does not make feature authoritative. main is precisely the version that was last agreed to work.

prompt: feature changed a.txt and main changed b.txt. feature is merged into main. What does main hold now?
optionA: The change to a.txt only
optionB: Both changes
optionC: The change to b.txt only
optionD: Neither, until somebody settles which is right
correctAnswerText: Both changes
explanation: The two branches touched different files, so main now holds both changes. There is nothing for anybody to choose between.

prompt: Immediately after that merge, what does feature hold?
optionA: Both changes, since the two branches are now joined
optionB: Nothing; its work moved into main
optionC: Both changes, once the merge has been sent
optionD: Its own change only; the merge did not alter it
correctAnswerText: Its own change only; the merge did not alter it
explanation: The merge wrote into main and left the source alone, so feature holds its own change only; the merge did not alter it. Giving feature main's work takes a merge in the other direction.

prompt: A developer working on feature expects to see their teammate's b.txt change and cannot find it. Both changes are present on main. What has happened?
optionA: The merge updated main only, and feature has never been given main's work
optionB: The merge stopped part way through
optionC: The b.txt change was discarded during the merge
optionD: feature has to be sent before it receives anything
correctAnswerText: The merge updated main only, and feature has never been given main's work
explanation: Both changes are on main, which shows the merge worked: the merge updated main only, and feature has never been given main's work. Merging main into feature is what would bring it across.

prompt: main runs c1, then c2, then c3. feature was started from c2 and has c4 and c5 on it. Which commits are on both branches?
optionA: c1, c2 and c3
optionB: All five of them
optionC: c1 and c2
optionD: None of them
correctAnswerText: c1 and c2
explanation: feature was started at c2 and everything up to that point came with it, so c1 and c2 are on both branches. c3 was added to main afterwards.

prompt: From that same pair of branches, which commits exist only on feature?
optionA: c3, c4 and c5
optionB: c4 and c5
optionC: c5 only
optionD: None; every commit is shared
correctAnswerText: c4 and c5
explanation: Only the commits made after the branch was started belong to it alone, so c4 and c5 exist only on feature. c3 belongs only to main, which is a different question.

prompt: A developer says the two branches went their separate ways at c3, because c3 is the newest commit on main. Where did they actually separate?
optionA: At c3, as the developer said
optionB: At c4, the first commit made on feature
optionC: At c1, where the project began
optionD: At c2, the last commit the two branches have in common
correctAnswerText: At c2, the last commit the two branches have in common
explanation: The separation is where the shared history stops, which is at c2, the last commit the two branches have in common. c3 was made on main after the branches had already parted.

prompt: One branch changed a.txt and the other changed b.txt. Does merging them clash?
optionA: No; changes to different files cannot compete
optionB: Yes; any two sets of changes have to be reconciled
optionC: Yes, if the two files sit in the same folder
optionD: Only if the files are large
correctAnswerText: No; changes to different files cannot compete
explanation: A clash needs two candidate versions of the same text, so no; changes to different files cannot compete. The merge completes without anybody being asked anything.

prompt: Both branches changed the same file: one edited the first line and the other edited the last line of a long file. Does merging clash?
optionA: Yes; both branches touched the same file
optionB: Yes; a file can only be changed on one branch at a time
optionC: No; the two edits are in different places in the file
optionD: Only if the two commits were made on the same day
correctAnswerText: No; the two edits are in different places in the file
explanation: Changes are compared region by region rather than file by file, so no; the two edits are in different places in the file. Both edits end up in the merged version.

prompt: Both branches changed the very same line of the very same file, and both changed it to the same text. Does merging clash?
optionA: Yes; the same line was written on both branches
optionB: No; there is nothing to choose between when the two results agree
optionC: Yes; identical edits on one line are the hardest case
optionD: Only if the two commit messages differ
correctAnswerText: No; there is nothing to choose between when the two results agree
explanation: A clash is a question that needs an answer, and the two branches already agree, so no; there is nothing to choose between when the two results agree. What produces a clash is two different texts competing for one place.

prompt: A merge has left a file holding a marked block: an opening marker, a line reading greeting = "Hello", a dividing marker, a line reading greeting = "Hi", and a closing marker. What must the resolved file contain?
optionA: Both greeting lines, with the markers kept as a record of what happened
optionB: Both greeting lines, with the markers taken out
optionC: Neither greeting line, with the markers taken out
optionD: One chosen greeting line, with all three marker lines taken out
correctAnswerText: One chosen greeting line, with all three marker lines taken out
explanation: Resolving means deciding what the file should say, so it must end with one chosen greeting line, with all three marker lines taken out. Keeping both would leave the variable set twice.

prompt: A marked block appears in a list of allowed countries: one branch added India to the list and the other added Kenya, at the same position. Both additions are wanted. What should the resolved list contain?
optionA: India and Kenya, one after the other, with the markers taken out
optionB: India only, with the markers taken out
optionC: Kenya only, since it was added on the branch being merged in
optionD: India and Kenya, with the markers left in to show the history
correctAnswerText: India and Kenya, one after the other, with the markers taken out
explanation: Marked blocks are not always a choice between alternatives, and here the list should hold India and Kenya, one after the other, with the markers taken out. Picking a side would silently drop a wanted entry.

prompt: A file was committed while it still contained the marker lines, and the project now refuses to run. What happened?
optionA: The merge broke the file as it was being written
optionB: The file was resolved while the wrong branch was current
optionC: The clash was recorded rather than settled, so the markers are now part of the file
optionD: The markers are harmless, so the failure has another cause
correctAnswerText: The clash was recorded rather than settled, so the markers are now part of the file
explanation: The markers are ordinary text as far as everything else is concerned, so the clash was recorded rather than settled, and the markers are now part of the file. Whatever reads the file meets lines it cannot make sense of.

prompt: A history splits into two lines after c2 and the two lines come back together at c6. How many lines of work does c6 draw on?
optionA: One
optionB: Two
optionC: Three
optionD: It cannot be told from the shape
correctAnswerText: Two
explanation: A point where two lines rejoin draws on both of them, so c6 draws on two. The split at c2 and the join at c6 are the two ends of the same pair of lines.

prompt: Somebody reads that shape as a single top-to-bottom sequence and concludes that c4 must have been written after c5. What have they missed?
optionA: The listing is printed with the oldest entry first
optionB: c4 and c5 were both made on the same branch
optionC: The point where the lines rejoined is where they had separated
optionD: The two lines ran alongside each other, so their commits are not in one single order
correctAnswerText: The two lines ran alongside each other, so their commits are not in one single order
explanation: A merged history is not a queue, so the two lines ran alongside each other, and their commits are not in one single order. c4 and c5 may have been written on the same afternoon by two people.

prompt: Yesterday's work does not appear on main. It does appear on feature, where the commits were made. What happened?
optionA: The work was committed onto the branch that was current at the time, which was not main
optionB: The work was lost when the branch was switched
optionC: main was reset to an earlier state
optionD: The work was never committed at all
correctAnswerText: The work was committed onto the branch that was current at the time, which was not main
explanation: The commits exist and they exist somewhere specific, so the work was committed onto the branch that was current at the time, which was not main. Merging is what puts it where it was wanted.

prompt: A file you wrote is not in the folder, the history of the current branch never mentions it, and a colleague can see it listed on another branch. What is the situation?
optionA: The work was deleted and will have to be written again
optionB: The shared copy has not been brought down recently enough
optionC: The work exists on that other branch, and this branch has simply never had it
optionD: The file was added to the ignore list by mistake
correctAnswerText: The work exists on that other branch, and this branch has simply never had it
explanation: A colleague seeing it on a branch settles that it was recorded, so the work exists on that other branch, and this branch has simply never had it. Nothing has been deleted and nothing needs fetching.

prompt: The export feature is finished and committed on a branch of its own, and it does not appear on main. What was not done?
optionA: The export work was never committed
optionB: The export branch was never merged into main
optionC: main was never sent to the shared copy
optionD: The export branch was deleted before it could be used
correctAnswerText: The export branch was never merged into main
explanation: The work is recorded and it is recorded elsewhere, so the export branch was never merged into main. Everything up to the merge was done.

prompt: main has been sent to the shared copy and the export feature still does not appear there. The export branch is itself committed and sent. What is missing?
optionA: The export commits, which were never made
optionB: A second send of the export branch
optionC: A fetch by whoever is looking at the shared copy
optionD: The merge; sending a branch does not put its work into another branch
correctAnswerText: The merge; sending a branch does not put its work into another branch
explanation: Both branches reached the shared copy and neither contains the other's work, so what is missing is the merge; sending a branch does not put its work into another branch. Sending and merging solve different problems.

prompt: Three branches were finished and only two of the three appear in main. Which check identifies the one that was left out?
optionA: Ask which branches have already been merged into main, rather than which branches have commits
optionB: Look at the newest commit message on main
optionC: Check that each of the three branches was sent to the shared copy
optionD: Compare how many commits each branch contains
correctAnswerText: Ask which branches have already been merged into main, rather than which branches have commits
explanation: Every branch has commits, so the presence of commits separates nothing: ask which branches have already been merged into main, rather than which branches have commits. Sending is irrelevant to whether main contains the work.

prompt: To be safe, somebody merges all three branches into main again. Two of them had already been merged. What happens to those two?
optionA: Their work is duplicated in the files
optionB: The merge is refused because they were merged once already
optionC: Nothing changes, because a merge that brings nothing new is not an error
optionD: Their earlier merges are undone and redone
correctAnswerText: Nothing changes, because a merge that brings nothing new is not an error
explanation: A merge brings across whatever the target does not already have, and here that is nothing, so nothing changes: a merge that brings nothing new is not an error. It is a safe thing to do and a poor way to find out what was missing.

prompt: A feature appears on the shared copy's main and not on your main. Both are called main. What is the explanation?
optionA: The feature was never merged into main at all
optionB: Your copy has not been given the newer commits that the shared copy holds
optionC: The feature was merged into the wrong branch
optionD: Two unrelated branches happen to share one name
correctAnswerText: Your copy has not been given the newer commits that the shared copy holds
explanation: The merge clearly happened, because the shared copy shows it, so your copy has not been given the newer commits that the shared copy holds. A branch name refers to a local line and a shared line that can be at different points.

prompt: Branches A and B both change the same line of one file, and both have to reach main. Every order listed below can be carried out. Which settles that line the fewest times?
optionA: Merge A into B, then B into main, then A into main as well
optionB: Merge B into A and A into B, then merge both into main
optionC: Merge A into main, then A into B, then B into main
optionD: Merge A into main, then merge B into main
correctAnswerText: Merge A into main, then merge B into main
explanation: The competing line has to be settled wherever the two meet, so merging A into main, then B into main brings them together exactly once. Every other order brings them together in a second place and asks the same question again.

prompt: A long-running branch can take main's newer work regularly, or wait and take it all at the end. What does waiting cost?
optionA: One large settlement at the end, over changes nobody remembers, instead of several small ones
optionB: Nothing; the same work is done either way
optionC: The branch becomes impossible to merge at all
optionD: The commits made on the branch are lost
correctAnswerText: One large settlement at the end, over changes nobody remembers, instead of several small ones
explanation: The total difference is the same and the shape of the work is not, so waiting buys one large settlement at the end, over changes nobody remembers, instead of several small ones. Deciding between two edits is far easier the week they were written.

prompt: During a series of merges, the very same competing line had to be settled twice. What does that tell you?
optionA: The first settlement was decided wrongly
optionB: The tool failed to record the first settlement
optionC: The merges were ordered so that the unsettled change was carried into two different places
optionD: Two people settled it differently at the same moment
correctAnswerText: The merges were ordered so that the unsettled change was carried into two different places
explanation: A settled line stays settled where it was settled, so the merges were ordered so that the unsettled change was carried into two different places. The repetition is a property of the route, not of the decision.

prompt: Why does merging each branch into main one at a time keep the settling in one place?
optionA: It is quicker than any other route
optionB: Every competing change meets the others where the work will finally live, and nowhere else
optionC: It removes the possibility of a clash
optionD: It allows the branches to be deleted sooner
correctAnswerText: Every competing change meets the others where the work will finally live, and nowhere else
explanation: Nothing is combined in an intermediate branch, so every competing change meets the others where the work will finally live, and nowhere else. Clashes still occur; each is simply decided once.

prompt: Some teams merge main into every feature branch daily, which keeps each settlement small. What does that habit cost?
optionA: Nothing; it is free and always worth doing
optionB: The branches can no longer be merged back into main
optionC: The settlements grow larger rather than smaller
optionD: Each branch fills up with merges that have nothing to do with the work it was made for
correctAnswerText: Each branch fills up with merges that have nothing to do with the work it was made for
explanation: The benefit is real and so is the price: each branch fills up with merges that have nothing to do with the work it was made for. Reading such a branch later means separating its own commits from everybody else's.

prompt: A single piece of work will take about two weeks and touches four files. Which branching approach fits it?
optionA: One branch for that piece of work, merged when it is finished
optionB: One branch for each of the four files
optionC: One branch for the developer, used for this and everything after it
optionD: No branch at all; commit the work straight onto main
correctAnswerText: One branch for that piece of work, merged when it is finished
explanation: The unit that gets merged should be the unit that is useful, which here is one branch for that piece of work, merged when it is finished. Four file branches would have to be merged together before any of them meant anything.

prompt: Some teams give each person one branch and keep it forever. That does work. What does it cost?
optionA: Nothing; it is simply easier to remember
optionB: Each person then needs a shared copy of their own
optionC: Two unrelated pieces of work share one branch, so neither can be merged until both are done
optionD: Clashes between people become impossible
correctAnswerText: Two unrelated pieces of work share one branch, so neither can be merged until both are done
explanation: The branch stops matching any unit of work, so two unrelated pieces of work share one branch, and neither can be merged until both are done. A finished feature waits behind an unfinished one for no reason.

prompt: Giving every file its own branch does make competing edits rare. What does it cost?
optionA: Nothing; smaller branches are better in every way
optionB: A change that spans three files becomes three branches that only work once all three are merged
optionC: Files can no longer be renamed or moved
optionD: The recorded history becomes shorter than it should be
correctAnswerText: A change that spans three files becomes three branches that only work once all three are merged
explanation: Rarity of clashes is bought at the price of coherence: a change that spans three files becomes three branches that only work once all three are merged. Any one of them merged alone leaves main broken.

prompt: What should decide how much work belongs on one branch?
optionA: The number of files the work touches
optionB: The number of people who will work on it
optionC: The number of days it is expected to take
optionD: The smallest amount that can be merged and still be worth having on its own
correctAnswerText: The smallest amount that can be merged and still be worth having on its own
explanation: A branch exists to be merged, so the measure is the smallest amount that can be merged and still be worth having on its own. Counting files, people or days describes the work rather than what makes it safe to combine.
